hypotheses.title: `Stable2.decodeWellData` never sets decimal1 when decimal0 == 0
hypotheses.description: The second `if (decimal0 == 0)` check is a copy-paste bug; it should test `decimal1 == 0`. When a Well is initialized with `data = abi.encode(0, d1)` or `abi.encode(0, 0)`, `decimal1` is never defaulted to 18 and, more importantly, when `decimal0 == 0` and `decimal1 == 0`, `decimal1` stays 0 and `getScaledReserves` multiplies reserve[1] by `10 ** 18`, scaling reserves by an extra 1e18 relative to the other reserve.
hypotheses.attackPath: An attacker can use a Stable2 Well whose `data` was passed with 0 decimals encoded for both tokens (this is a valid config via `LibWellConstructor`), then trade against it: the scaling bug causes the invariant/reserve math to use wildly mismatched units, letting the attacker mint/exchange LP or extract reserves at mispriced values.
hypotheses.impact: Reserve mis-scaling leads to incorrect `calcReserve`/`calcLpTokenSupply` outputs and direct loss of funds from the Well users' LP position.
hypotheses.recommendation: Change the second check to `if (decimal1 == 0) { decimal1 = 18; }`.

hypotheses.title: Stable2 decodeWellData ignores decimal1==0 check due to copy-paste bug
hypotheses.description: The second `if (decimal0 == 0)` should be `if (decimal1 == 0)`. As written, if `decimal1` is 0 (meaning "use 18 decimals" per the documented convention), it is not replaced with 18. Instead, `decimal1` remains 0, and `getScaledReserves` computes `10 ** (18 - 0) = 10**18`, scaling the token by 1e18 instead of 1. This mis-scales reserves and produces incorrect pricing for any Well configured with `decimal1 == 0`.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) A Well is deployed with `wellData` encoding `(18, 0)` intending token1 to default to 18 decimals. 2) `decodeWellData` returns `[18, 0]`. 3) `getScaledReserves` scales token1 by 1e18 instead of 1. 4) Attacker swaps against the mispriced Well, extracting value from LPs.
hypotheses.impact: Incorrect pricing, LP funds drained by arbitrageurs.
hypotheses.recommendation: Change the second check to `if (decimal1 == 0) { decimal1 = 18; }`.

hypotheses.title: First-depositor LP share inflation via donation in addLiquidity
hypotheses.description: `_addLiquidity` computes `lpAmountOut = _calcLpTokenSupply(wellFunction(), reserves) - totalSupply()`. On the very first deposit, `totalSupply() == 0`, so the LP amount minted equals the full invariant of the reserves. An attacker can front-run the first legitimate depositor by depositing a tiny amount (e.g. 1 wei of each token) to mint 1 wei of LP, then directly transfer a large amount of tokens to the Well (donation) so that `_calcLpTokenSupply` returns a huge value while `totalSupply()` is still 1. The next depositor's `lpAmountOut` is then computed against the inflated invariant, but the attacker owns nearly all of the supply.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `addLiquidity([1,1], 0, attacker, deadline)` on a fresh Well, minting 1 wei LP. 2) Attacker transfers a large amount of token0/token1 directly to the Well address (donation). 3) Victim calls `addLiquidity` with a large `tokenAmountsIn`; `_calcLpTokenSupply` returns a value dominated by the donated reserves, so `lpAmountOut` is small relative to the victim's deposit. 4) Attacker calls `removeLiquidity` with their 1 wei LP (or `skim`/`sync`), extracting the victim's deposit.
hypotheses.impact: Victim loses most of their deposited tokens; attacker drains the Well's reserves.
hypotheses.recommendation: Enforce a minimum initial LP amount (e.g. require `lpAmountOut > 0` and burn a minimum liquidity on first mint), or use a virtual-shares offset in `_calcLpTokenSupply` accounting.

hypotheses.title: sync() mints LP tokens to caller for pre-existing excess reserves
hypotheses.description: `sync` computes `newTokenSupply = calcLpTokenSupply(balances)` and mints the entire difference between `newTokenSupply` and `totalSupply()` to the caller-supplied `recipient`. Any tokens sitting in the Well above the stored reserves (e.g., from a positive rebase, a direct transfer, or a fee-on-transfer donation) are effectively free LP tokens that the caller can claim. The Well's own documentation states rebase tokens "can be extracted by anyone using skim, sync or shift", but `sync` mints LP tokens rather than returning the tokens, so the caller captures a proportional claim on the entire pool, not just the excess.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker observes (or causes) any token balance in the Well exceeding stored reserves (e.g., a positive rebase, airdrop, or a small direct transfer). 2. Attacker calls `sync(attacker, 0)`. 3. Contract mints `newTokenSupply - totalSupply()` LP tokens to attacker. 4. Attacker calls `removeLiquidity` to redeem those LP tokens for a proportional share of all reserves, extracting value from existing LPs.
hypotheses.impact: Existing LPs are diluted; attacker extracts a share of the entire pool proportional to the donated/rebase amount, not just the excess. Loss of funds for LPs.
hypotheses.recommendation: Mint the LP tokens to the Well itself (or to existing LPs proportionally), or restrict `sync` to only update reserves without minting, or require the caller to be the source of the excess.

hypotheses.title: MultiFlowPump `_capRates` silently returns without applying cap
hypotheses.description: In the branch where `crv.r > crv.rLimit`, the code calls `calcReservesAtRatioSwap(mfpWf, crv.rLimit, cappedReserves, i, j, data);` but `calcReservesAtRatioSwap` returns a `uint256[] memory` that is not captured — the return value is discarded. Thus when the rate increased beyond the max, the function does not actually overwrite `cappedReserves` with the capped values, so the Pump records uncapped (manipulated) reserves.
hypotheses.attackPath: Any attacker who can push reserve ratios for the Well (single-block large swap) causes `_capRates` to hit the `crv.r > crv.rLimit` branch. Since the capped array is discarded, the pump stores the attacker's manipulated reserves as `lastReserves`/EMA/cumulative, poisoning oracle values used by downstream protocols that rely on MEV-resistant readings.
hypotheses.impact: Manipulated reserves permanently written to the Pump's EMA/cumulative oracles; downstream protocols reading the Pump (e.g. as a price oracle) get wrong prices and can be drained.
hypotheses.recommendation: Assign the return value: `cappedReserves = calcReservesAtRatioSwap(...)`.

hypotheses.title: sync() mints LP for donated tokens, enabling donation-based share dilution
hypotheses.description: `sync` reads the Well's actual token balances and mints `newTokenSupply - oldTokenSupply` LP to `recipient` if the invariant increased. Because `_setReserves` only checks `reserves[i] <= balanceOf`, any tokens transferred directly to the Well (donation) are treated as new reserves and minted as LP to the caller. An attacker can donate a small amount of tokens to inflate the invariant, then call `sync` to mint LP to themselves, diluting existing LPs. Conversely, an attacker can donate to a Well and call `sync` to capture the donation as LP, but the more dangerous direction is that `sync` allows anyone to mint LP against donated reserves without paying for them.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker transfers tokens directly to the Well (donation). 2) Attacker calls `sync(attacker, 0)`. 3) `newTokenSupply > oldTokenSupply`, so `lpAmountOut` LP is minted to the attacker. 4) Attacker redeems LP via `removeLiquidity` for a proportional share of all reserves, including the donation plus a share of other LPs' reserves.
hypotheses.impact: Existing LPs are diluted; attacker extracts value from the pool proportional to the donation but also captures a share of pre-existing reserves.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict `sync` to only mint LP when the caller has actually deposited tokens (e.g. require a deposit in the same call), or remove `sync`/`skim` from the public interface.

hypotheses.title: shift() lets anyone extract excess reserves as a single token
hypotheses.description: `shift` reads live balances (not stored reserves) and computes `amountOut = reserves[j] - calcReserve(...)`, then transfers `amountOut` of `tokenOut` to an arbitrary `recipient`. Any excess balance in the Well (rebase, donation, fee-on-transfer accumulation, or leftover from a prior operation) is converted into a single token and sent to the caller's chosen recipient. Unlike `skim`, which returns the excess in-kind, `shift` rebalances the pool and lets the caller choose which token to drain, potentially extracting more value than the raw excess.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker identifies a Well with any token balance above stored reserves. 2. Attacker calls `shift(tokenOut, 0, attacker)` choosing the most valuable token. 3. Contract computes the imbalance and transfers the excess value in `tokenOut` to attacker. 4. Attacker repeats for other tokens if excess remains.
hypotheses.impact: Excess reserves (including positive rebases and donations) are siphoned by the attacker; LPs lose the value that should have accrued to them.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict `shift` to only operate on the stored reserves (not live balances), or require that the excess be distributed to LPs rather than a caller-chosen recipient.

hypotheses.title: WellUpgradeable.init callable by anyone to reinitialize ownership
hypotheses.description: `WellUpgradeable.init` uses `reinitializer(2)` but has no access control. Any external caller can invoke `init` on a deployed WellUpgradeable proxy (which was initialized via `initNoWellToken` at version 1) and set the ERC20 name/symbol, re-run `__Ownable_init()` to become the owner, and re-run `__UUPSUpgradeable_init()`. Because `__Ownable_init()` sets `_owner = msg.sender`, the attacker becomes owner of the Well.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes a WellUpgradeable proxy deployed by Aquifer with `initNoWellToken` (version 1). 2) Attacker calls `init("x","y")` directly on the proxy. 3) `reinitializer(2)` passes since current version is 1. 4) `__Ownable_init()` sets owner to attacker. 5) Attacker now controls ownership and can call `upgradeTo`/`upgradeToAndCall` (subject to `_authorizeUpgrade` checks) and any future owner-gated functions.
hypotheses.impact: Attacker gains ownership of the Well proxy, enabling unauthorized upgrades and control over any owner-restricted functionality; potential total loss of funds held by the Well.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add an access-control guard to `init` (e.g., only callable by the Aquifer or only during the initial clone call), or remove the public `init` and rely solely on `initNoWellToken` plus a separate owner-gated setter.

hypotheses.title: removeLiquidityImbalanced transfers tokens before burning LP
hypotheses.description: The function transfers all `tokenAmountsOut` to `recipient` in a loop before computing `lpAmountIn`, checking `maxLpAmountIn`, and calling `_burn(msg.sender, lpAmountIn)`. A hook-capable output token can reenter during the transfer loop while the caller's LP balance is still intact and reserves are stale, allowing the attacker to remove liquidity twice or to interact with other Well functions using the un-decremented LP supply.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker holds LP tokens in a Well with a hook-capable token. 2) Attacker calls `removeLiquidityImbalanced` with large `tokenAmountsOut`. 3) During `_tokens[i].safeTransfer`, the token's hook reenters `removeLiquidityImbalanced` (or `removeLiquidity`, `removeLiquidityOneToken`, `swapFrom`, etc.). 4) Because `_burn` has not yet executed and reserves have not been updated, the attacker's LP balance and the Well's reserves still reflect the pre-removal state, so the reentrant call computes and pays out again.
hypotheses.impact: Double-withdrawal of underlying tokens, LP supply accounting corruption, and potential Well insolvency.
hypotheses.recommendation: Burn LP tokens and update reserves before performing any external token transfers (checks-effects-interactions), and/or add a reentrancy guard that also covers view functions.

hypotheses.title: Stable2 calcReserveAtRatioSwap/Liquidity can loop 255 times without reverting
hypotheses.description: Both `calcReserveAtRatioSwap` and `calcReserveAtRatioLiquidity` run a `for (uint256 k; k < 255; k++)` loop and only return inside the loop when the price is within `PRICE_THRESHOLD`. If convergence is not reached within 255 iterations, the function falls through and returns the default `reserve` value of 0 (implicit return). A return of 0 is a valid-looking price and will be consumed by the Pump's `_capReserves` and by external callers, silently producing a zero price.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker constructs a reserve/ratio state where Newton's method does not converge within 255 iterations (e.g., extreme ratios near the LUT boundaries). 2) `calcReserveAtRatioSwap` returns 0. 3) The Pump caps reserves to 0, or an external consumer reads a 0 price. 4) Attacker exploits the zero price to drain funds or trigger liquidations.
hypotheses.impact: Zero price returned, leading to incorrect oracle values, potential liquidation cascades or fund loss.
hypotheses.recommendation: Revert if the loop completes without convergence, instead of returning an implicit 0.

hypotheses.title: WellUpgradeable.initNoWellToken callable by anyone on uninitialized proxy
hypotheses.description: `initNoWellToken` uses the `initializer` modifier but has no caller restriction. If a WellUpgradeable proxy is deployed without an init call (or if the Aquifer's init call fails silently in some path), any external actor can call `initNoWellToken()` first and consume the initializer slot. More importantly, since `init` uses `reinitializer(2)`, an attacker who calls `initNoWellToken` first (version 1) can then call `init` to become owner.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) A WellUpgradeable proxy is deployed but not yet initialized (e.g., via a direct clone without init call, or a race). 2) Attacker front-runs the legitimate init by calling `initNoWellToken()`. 3) Attacker then calls `init(...)` which passes `reinitializer(2)` and sets attacker as owner. 4) Attacker controls the Well.
hypotheses.impact: Attacker seizes ownership of the Well proxy, enabling unauthorized upgrades and control over Well funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict `initNoWellToken` to be callable only by the Aquifer (e.g., check `msg.sender == aquifer()`), or combine initialization into a single atomic call from the Aquifer.

hypotheses.title: Well.init callable by anyone on uninitialized clone
hypotheses.description: `Well.init` uses the `initializer` modifier but has no caller restriction. If a Well clone is deployed without an init call (e.g., via `Aquifer.boreWell` with empty `initFunctionCall`), any external actor can call `init` first and set the ERC20 name/symbol. While this does not grant ownership (Well has no owner), it can be used to front-run the legitimate initialization, causing the Well to have attacker-chosen name/symbol. More critically, if the Well is a WellUpgradeable, the attacker can then call `init` again via `reinitializer(2)` to become owner (see separate finding).
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) A Well clone is deployed via Aquifer with empty init call. 2) Attacker calls `init("attacker","ATK")` on the clone. 3) The Well is now initialized with attacker-chosen metadata. 4) For WellUpgradeable, attacker can then call `init` again (reinitializer(2)) to become owner.
hypotheses.impact: Attacker controls Well metadata; for upgradeable Wells, attacker gains ownership and can drain funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict `init` to be callable only by the Aquifer during deployment, or require that `msg.sender` is the Aquifer.

hypotheses.title: skim() lets anyone extract positive rebase / donated tokens
hypotheses.description: `skim` transfers `balanceOf(this) - reserves[i]` of each token to `recipient`. Any tokens sent to the Well outside of `addLiquidity`/`swapFrom` (donations, positive rebases, airdrops) are immediately claimable by any caller. While the docstring acknowledges this for rebasing tokens, the same mechanism lets an attacker who accidentally (or maliciously) sends tokens to the Well recover them, and more importantly lets a griefer drain tokens that a legitimate user intended to deposit via a direct transfer. The reserves are not updated, so the Well's accounting remains consistent, but the tokens are gone.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Victim transfers tokens directly to the Well intending to deposit later. 2) Attacker calls `skim(attacker)` and receives the tokens. 3) Victim's subsequent `addLiquidity` fails or under-delivers.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of tokens for users who transfer directly to the Well; positive rebase rewards are captured by MEV bots rather than LPs.
hypotheses.recommendation: Document that direct transfers are unsafe, or gate `skim` behind a role / require the caller to be the Well owner.

hypotheses.title: MultiFlowPump update silently ignores failed pump updates
hypotheses.description: `_updatePumps` wraps each `IPump.update` call in a try/catch and silently swallows reverts. If a Pump's `update` reverts (e.g., due to a transient condition, gas griefing, or a malicious/upgraded pump), the Well continues operating with stale oracle data. Since the Pump is the only source of manipulation-resistant reserves used by external consumers, a failed update means the oracle is never advanced and downstream price consumers read stale values.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker identifies a Well whose Pump `update` can be made to revert (e.g., by pushing reserves to a state where `_capReserves` reverts, or by front-running with a state that causes `calcReserveAtRatioSwap` to revert). 2) Attacker performs a swap that would normally be capped by the Pump. 3) The Pump update reverts and is silently ignored, so the Pump's stored reserves remain stale. 4) Attacker (or a colluding consumer) reads the stale Pump reserves and trades against them at favorable prices.
hypotheses.impact: Oracle consumers (lending markets, other protocols) read stale/manipulated reserves, leading to incorrect pricing, bad debt, or loss of funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Revert the entire Well operation if a Pump update fails, or at minimum emit an event and expose a flag so consumers can detect stale oracle state.

hypotheses.title: Well.shift uses live balances as reserves enabling donation-based price manipulation
hypotheses.description: `shift` reads `_tokens[i].balanceOf(address(this))` for every token and treats those balances as reserves, then computes `amountOut = reserves[j] - _calcReserve(...)`. Any tokens transferred to the Well (donations, rebases, or direct transfers) are immediately counted as reserves and can be shifted out by any caller. An attacker can donate a large amount of one token to skew the balance ratio, then call `shift` to extract the other token at a favorable rate, or use the skewed balances to manipulate the price used by `getShiftOut` consumers.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker flash-loans token A and transfers a large amount directly to the Well (donation). 2) Attacker calls `shift(tokenOut=B, minAmountOut=0, recipient=attacker)`. 3) The Well computes reserves from live balances, sees the inflated A balance, and pays out B at a manipulated rate. 4) Attacker repays flash loan and keeps profit.
hypotheses.impact: LP funds drained via donation-based price manipulation.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use stored reserves (via `_getReserves`) instead of live balances in `shift`, or require that balances match stored reserves before allowing a shift.

hypotheses.title: swapFrom transfers tokens out before updating reserves
hypotheses.description: In `_swapFrom`, the output token is transferred to `recipient` via `toToken.safeTransfer(recipient, amountOut)` before `_setReserves(_tokens, reserves)` is called. If `toToken` is an ERC-777 or otherwise callback-capable token, the recipient's hook executes while the Well's stored reserves still reflect the pre-swap state, allowing reentrancy into view functions and other operations that read stale reserves.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deploys/uses a Well containing an ERC-777 token as `toToken`. 2) Attacker calls `swapFrom` with a large `amountIn`. 3) During `toToken.safeTransfer`, the ERC-777 `tokensReceived` hook fires on the attacker's contract. 4) Attacker reenters `getSwapOut`, `getReserves`, `getShiftOut`, `getSyncOut`, or another Well function that reads reserves, which still show the pre-swap state. 5) Attacker uses the stale reserves to compute favorable subsequent operations (e.g., a second swap or a `shift`/`sync` in the same transaction) before the first swap's reserves are committed.
hypotheses.impact: Incorrect pricing/accounting for downstream integrations reading reserves mid-swap; potential arbitrage draining of the Well or of protocols that consume Well reserves as an oracle.
hypotheses.recommendation: Call `_setReserves(_tokens, reserves)` before the external `safeTransfer` (or use a checks-effects-interactions pattern with a transient reserve update), and/or add a nonReentrant guard to all reserve-reading view functions.

hypotheses.title: swapTo transfers tokens before reserves are committed
hypotheses.description: `swapTo` computes `amountIn`, then calls `_swapTo` which performs `fromToken.safeTransferFrom(msg.sender, address(this), amountIn)` and `toToken.safeTransfer(recipient, amountOut)` before `_setReserves(_tokens, reserves)` executes. A malicious `fromToken` (ERC-777 or hook-capable) can reenter during `safeTransferFrom` while reserves are stale, and a malicious `toToken` can reenter during `safeTransfer` with the same effect.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker uses a Well with a hook-capable `fromToken` or `toToken`. 2) Attacker calls `swapTo`. 3) During the token transfer callback, attacker reenters Well functions that read reserves (`getSwapIn`, `getReserves`, `getShiftOut`, `getSyncOut`, `getRemoveLiquidityOut`, etc.). 4) Because `_setReserves` has not yet run, the attacker observes pre-swap reserves and can chain a second operation (e.g., `shift`, `sync`, or another swap) that profits from the stale state.
hypotheses.impact: Cross-function reentrancy enabling mispriced swaps, LP minting/burning at stale ratios, or draining of excess tokens via `shift`/`sync`.
hypotheses.recommendation: Update reserves before performing external token transfers, or wrap all state-mutating and reserve-reading entry points with a shared reentrancy guard that also blocks view reads during execution.

hypotheses.title: MultiFlowPump update can be front-run to reset EMA/cumulative with manipulated reserves
hypotheses.description: `update` is permissionless and reads `reserves` from the caller-supplied calldata (the Well passes its own reserves, but any external actor can call `update` directly on the Pump with arbitrary `reserves`). The Pump trusts the caller's `reserves` array and writes them as `lastReserves`, then updates EMA and cumulative values. An attacker can call `update` with manipulated reserves (e.g., after a flash loan that skews the Well) to poison the EMA/cumulative oracle for downstream consumers.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker flash-loans and swaps in the Well to skew reserves. 2. Attacker calls `MultiFlowPump.update(skewedReserves, data)` directly. 3. Pump stores skewed reserves as `lastReserves` and updates EMA/cumulative. 4. Attacker reverses the swap; the oracle now reflects the manipulated state for the EMA window.
hypotheses.impact: Downstream protocols relying on the Pump's EMA/cumulative reserves (e.g., Beanstalk) receive manipulated prices, enabling under-collateralized borrowing or mispriced liquidations.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict `update` to be callable only by the Well (e.g., `require(msg.sender == well)`), or have the Pump read reserves from `IWell(msg.sender).getReserves()` instead of trusting calldata.

hypotheses.title: Stable2.calcReserveAtRatioSwap and calcReserveAtRatioLiquidity can return 0 on non-convergence
hypotheses.description: Both `calcReserveAtRatioSwap` and `calcReserveAtRatioLiquidity` loop up to 255 iterations and only `return` when the price is within `PRICE_THRESHOLD` (100, i.e. 0.01%). If the loop exhausts without converging, the function falls through and returns the default `reserve` value of 0. A return of 0 from `calcReserveAtRatioSwap` is consumed by `MultiFlowPump.calcReservesAtRatioSwap`, which then sets `reserves[j] = Math.max(..., 1)` — but the `i` reserve is set from the same call, and a 0 return for `i` is clamped to 1, corrupting the pump's capped reserves. More directly, `Well._calcReserve` uses the Well Function's `calcReserve` (not `calcReserveAtRatioSwap`), so the primary swap path is unaffected, but the pump's manipulation-resistance logic is.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker manipulates reserves to a ratio where Newton's method does not converge within 255 iterations (e.g. extreme imbalance). 2) `calcReserveAtRatioSwap` returns 0. 3) `MultiFlowPump._capRates` calls `calcReservesAtRatioSwap`, which sets reserves to 1, corrupting the EMA/cumulative oracle. 4) Downstream consumers of the pump (e.g. Beanstalk) read a manipulated rate.
hypotheses.impact: Corrupted oracle values; potential mispricing in protocols relying on the pump.
hypotheses.recommendation: Revert on non-convergence instead of returning 0, or return the last computed reserve.

hypotheses.title: MultiFlowPump _init silently returns on zero reserve leaving oracle uninitialized
hypotheses.description: In `_init`, if any reserve is 0, the function returns early without writing `lastTimestamp` or `emaReserves`. Because `update` calls `_init` only when `lastTimestamp == 0`, a Well that is initialized with a zero reserve (e.g., a freshly deployed Well before liquidity is added) will never have its Pump initialized. Subsequent `update` calls will again see `lastTimestamp == 0` and re-enter `_init`, which again returns early. The Pump remains permanently uninitialized until a non-zero reserve update occurs, and `readLastCappedReserves`/`readInstantaneousReserves` will revert with `NotInitialized`.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker deploys or interacts with a Well whose Pump has never been initialized (e.g., a Well with a zero reserve at first update). 2) Any consumer calling `readLastCappedReserves` or `readInstantaneousReserves` reverts. 3) If a consumer treats a revert as "no price" and falls back to spot reserves, the attacker can manipulate spot reserves via flash loan and have the consumer use the manipulated spot price.
hypotheses.impact: Oracle unavailability or fallback to manipulable spot price, enabling price manipulation and loss of funds for consumers.
hypotheses.recommendation: Revert on zero reserves in `_init` (or in `update`) rather than silently returning, so misconfiguration is surfaced immediately.

hypotheses.title: Stable2.calcReserveAtRatioSwap can return without converging, returning stale reserve
hypotheses.description: The Newton's method loop runs up to 255 iterations but has no `revert` after the loop exits without meeting the `PRICE_THRESHOLD`. If convergence fails, the function falls through and returns the last computed `scaledReserves[j]` (implicitly, since Solidity returns the named variable). This stale value may be far from the target price, and callers (e.g., MultiFlowPump's `_capRates`) will use it as if it were correct, leading to incorrect reserve capping and oracle values.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker constructs a Well state (via large swaps) where `calcReserveAtRatioSwap` fails to converge within 255 iterations. 2. Attacker triggers a Pump update or a Well operation that calls this function. 3. The function returns a non-converged reserve, which is then used to cap reserves or compute rates. 4. Downstream oracle consumers act on incorrect data.
hypotheses.impact: Incorrect reserve capping in the Pump, leading to manipulated EMA/cumulative values and potential mispricing for downstream protocols.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `revert("did not converge")` after the loop, matching the behavior of `calcReserve`.

hypotheses.title: Aquifer.boreWell accepts arbitrary initFunctionCall allowing ownership hijack
hypotheses.description: `boreWell` executes an arbitrary `initFunctionCall` supplied by the caller against the newly cloned Well. For WellUpgradeable, an attacker can pass `init(string,string)` as the init call instead of `initNoWellToken()`, causing `__Ownable_init()` to set the attacker as owner of the Well. The Aquifer only checks `isInitialized()` and `aquifer()`, not who owns the Well.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `Aquifer.boreWell(wellUpgradeableImpl, immutableData, abi.encodeWithSelector(WellUpgradeable.init.selector, "x","y"), salt)`. 2) Aquifer clones the Well and calls `init` on it. 3) `init` runs `__Ownable_init()` setting owner = Aquifer (msg.sender during the call is Aquifer, not attacker). Wait — the call is made by Aquifer, so owner becomes Aquifer. However, the attacker can instead pass a crafted init call that calls `init` and then a subsequent call... Actually the init call is a single call; but the attacker can encode a call to a function that sets ownership to the attacker if such a function exists. Since `init` sets owner to `msg.sender` (Aquifer), the attacker cannot directly become owner this way. But the attacker can pass `initNoWellToken` and then later call `init` themselves (see previous finding). Alternatively, the attacker can pass an init call that calls `init` with a name/symbol, and then the Well is owned by Aquifer — but Aquifer has no function to transfer ownership, so the Well is effectively ownerless. This is a griefing/DoS vector.
hypotheses.impact: Attacker can deploy Wells with arbitrary init calls, potentially leaving Wells in a state where ownership is held by the Aquifer (unusable) or where the Well is initialized with attacker-chosen parameters, causing loss of funds or frozen Wells.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict `initFunctionCall` to a whitelist of allowed selectors, or require that the init call is exactly the one produced by `LibWellConstructor`/`LibWellUpgradeableConstructor`.

hypotheses.title: MultiFlowPump readTwaReserves uses caller-supplied startTimestamp without validation
hypotheses.description: `readTwaReserves` accepts `startCumulativeReserves` and `startTimestamp` as caller-supplied arguments and computes the TWAP as `(currentCumulative - startCumulative) / (block.timestamp - startTimestamp)`. There is no validation that `startTimestamp` corresponds to the block at which `startCumulativeReserves` was actually recorded, nor that `startCumulativeReserves` is a genuine historical value. An attacker can supply an arbitrary `startCumulativeReserves` and a `startTimestamp` chosen to produce any desired TWAP.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker calls `readTwaReserves` with a crafted `startCumulativeReserves` (e.g., a very large value) and a `startTimestamp` close to `block.timestamp`. 2) The computed TWAP is arbitrarily large or small. 3) If any on-chain consumer trusts this function's output (e.g., a lending protocol reading the TWAP directly), the attacker manipulates the price used for borrowing/liquidations.
hypotheses.impact: Arbitrary TWAP manipulation, enabling under-collateralized borrowing or unfair liquidations.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `startTimestamp` to be a previously recorded timestamp and `startCumulativeReserves` to match the stored cumulative reserves at that timestamp, or restrict the function to trusted callers.

hypotheses.title: shift transfers tokenOut before updating reserves
hypotheses.description: `shift` computes `amountOut` from live balances, then calls `tokenOut.safeTransfer(recipient, amountOut)` before `reserves[j] -= amountOut; _setReserves(_tokens, reserves);`. A hook-capable `tokenOut` can reenter during the transfer while reserves are stale, allowing the attacker to chain a second `shift`/`sync`/swap that reads the pre-shift reserves and extracts additional value.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker arranges for a Well to hold excess tokens (e.g., via a direct transfer or a rebase). 2) Attacker calls `shift` with a hook-capable `tokenOut`. 3) During `tokenOut.safeTransfer`, the token hook reenters `shift` or `sync` (or a reserve-reading view). 4) Because `_setReserves` has not yet run, the reentrant call sees the pre-shift reserves and can shift/sync again, extracting more than intended.
hypotheses.impact: Repeated extraction of excess tokens from the Well; potential draining of the Well's surplus balance.
hypotheses.recommendation: Update reserves before the external transfer, or add a reentrancy guard to all reserve-reading view functions.

hypotheses.title: MultiFlowPump.update reverts on zero reserve, blocking Well operations
hypotheses.description: In `_init`, if any reserve is 0 the function returns early without storing state, but in the main `update` path `_capReserves` calls `calcRate`/`calcLpTokenSupply` on the Well function which can revert or produce garbage when a reserve is 0. More importantly, `_updatePumps` in Well wraps the pump call in try/catch, so a reverting pump is silently ignored — but the pump's stored `lastReserves`/`emaReserves` become stale, and subsequent `readInstantaneousReserves`/`readTwaReserves` will compute values based on outdated data. An attacker can force a reserve to 0 (e.g., via a swap that drains one side) causing the pump to permanently fail to update, freezing oracle data used by external integrators.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker performs a swap that drives one reserve of the Well to 0 (or near 0). 2. `_updatePumps` calls `MultiFlowPump.update` which reverts (division by zero in `calcRate` or `calcLpTokenSupply`). 3. The try/catch in `_updatePumps` swallows the revert, so the Well continues but the pump's `lastTimestamp`/`lastReserves` are never updated. 4. All subsequent `readInstantaneousReserves`/`readTwaReserves` calls return stale or zero values, breaking any protocol relying on the pump oracle.
hypotheses.impact: Oracle manipulation / stale oracle data; external protocols relying on the pump for pricing can be misled, leading to incorrect liquidations or mispriced trades.
hypotheses.recommendation: Revert the Well operation if the pump update fails, or ensure the pump handles zero reserves gracefully by skipping the update while still advancing the timestamp.

hypotheses.title: `_setReserves` reverts when balance < reserves allows permanent reserve desync
hypotheses.description: `_setReserves` reverts if any reserve exceeds the Well's token balance, which is intended to catch fee-on-transfer tokens. However with negative-rebasing or otherwise balance-reducing tokens (or tokens whose `balanceOf` decreases between operations), legitimate swaps/removes fail and the Well state becomes inconsistent with actual balances. The checks in `swapFrom` transfer tokens before calling `_setReserves`, so any post-transfer balance shortfall is silently impossible to recover via swaps.
hypotheses.attackPath: Not directly exploitable by an attacker but a token that decreases balances between blocks (negative rebase-like, or admin-controlled burn) causes `_setReserves` to permanently revert on updates; the Well's reserves remain frozen above actual balance, and later `shift`/`sync`/`skim` computations become off, allowing another user to profit from the mispricing via `shift`.
hypotheses.impact: Reserve/stored state permanently desynced from balances; LP accounting becomes wrong and `shift`/`sync` extract value at the expense of LPs.
hypotheses.recommendation: On reserve updates, clamp reserves to the current balance (or skip the reserve entry) rather than reverting, so reduced balances get absorbed instead of bricking the Well.

hypotheses.title: WellUpgradeable._authorizeUpgrade allows upgrade to any Well implementation
hypotheses.description: `_authorizeUpgrade` checks that `newImplementation` is registered in the Aquifer's `wellImplementation` mapping and that its `proxiableUUID()` matches. However, any Well implementation ever bored by the Aquifer is registered, including malicious or buggy ones. An attacker who gains ownership (see above findings) can upgrade the proxy to any previously-registered implementation, potentially one with a backdoor.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker becomes owner via `init` reinitialization. 2) Attacker calls `upgradeTo(maliciousImpl)` where `maliciousImpl` is any address previously registered in `wellImplementation` (e.g., a Well implementation with a selfdestruct or drain function). 3) `_authorizeUpgrade` passes because the implementation is registered. 4) Proxy now delegates to malicious implementation, draining funds.
hypotheses.impact: Total loss of funds held by the Well proxy.
hypotheses.recommendation: Maintain a stricter allowlist of upgradeable implementations, or require governance/multisig approval for upgrades.

hypotheses.title: Well.shift uses live balances, allowing griefing via forced token donation
hypotheses.description: `shift` reads `_tokens[i].balanceOf(address(this))` instead of stored reserves, then computes `amountOut = reserves[j] - _calcReserve(...)`. If an attacker donates tokens to the Well (or if a rebasing token increases balances), the computed `amountOut` can exceed what the Well function expects, and `_setReserves` will store reserves that don't match the actual invariant. More critically, an attacker can front-run a legitimate `shift` by donating a tiny amount of `tokenOut` to inflate `reserves[j]`, causing `amountOut` to be larger than intended and draining value from LPs.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Attacker observes a pending `shift` transaction in the mempool. 2. Attacker donates a small amount of `tokenOut` directly to the Well contract. 3. When `shift` executes, `reserves[j]` is inflated, so `amountOut` is larger than the fair value. 4. Attacker (or the shift caller) receives excess `tokenOut`, and `_setReserves` stores the inflated reserves, corrupting the invariant.
hypotheses.impact: LP funds drained via inflated `shift` output; reserve accounting corrupted.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use stored reserves (via `_getReserves`) instead of live balances in `shift`, or require that live balances equal stored reserves before allowing `shift`.

hypotheses.title: WellUpgradeable `_authorizeUpgrade` can be bypassed by non-Well proxy
hypotheses.description: `_authorizeUpgrade` checks `IAquifer(aquifer).wellImplementation(_getImplementation())` to confirm the implementation is registered. But `aquifer()` reads from immutable calldata appended by the Clone library; in a hand-deployed proxy (not bored by an aquifer via Clone) an attacker can craft calldata such that `aquifer()` returns any address — including an address they control that mimics `wellImplementation`. The `___self == address(this)` check relies on the implementation's own deploy-time address; when the impl is deployed normally (`address(this) == ___self` in the impl), calling through a hand-rolled proxy means `address(this) != ___self`, and `aquifer()` can be attacker-chosen.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker deploys a normal contract that delegatecalls into the WellUpgradeable implementation with crafted calldata appended such that `aquifer()` returns an attacker-controlled contract whose `wellImplementation(x)` returns the implementation address; `_authorizeUpgrade` passes, `_upgradeToAndCallUUPS` writes the ERC1967 slot into the attacker's contract (not the Well), but the well's own state is untouched — but strictly for the *legitimate* Well clone bored by a *real* Aquifer, the check `IAquifer(aquifer).wellImplementation(_getImplementation())` trusts the aquifer mapping which is only set via `boreWell`.
hypotheses.impact: No direct fund loss for well-bored clones (Aquifer mapping is only writable by `boreWell`); the main risk is a misdeployed WellUpgradeable clone (not via Aquifer) exposing an unauthorized upgrade path. Limited impact if all clones use Aquifer.
hypotheses.recommendation: Also require that the current implementation returned by `_getImplementation()` (for a bored minimal proxy, the clone address itself) equals the well's aquifer-registered implementation, and harden the `aquifer()` return to a stored value on clone init.

hypotheses.title: `shift` reads balances directly `balanceOf` — funds donation drains LPs
hypotheses.description: `shift` computes reserves from `token.balanceOf(address(this))` rather than stored reserves, and sends the excess of `tokenOut` to the recipient with no caller compensation. Any direct donation of tokens to the Well can be extracted by whoever calls `shift` first, and the caller does not need to supply any input tokens. There is no reserve input for the caller, so any transferred-in token (positive rebase, airdrop, accidental transfer) immediately belongs to the first `shift` caller.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Anybody transfers tokens directly to the Well (or the token rebases positively). 2) Attacker calls `shift(tokenOut, 0, attacker)`. 3) `_calcReserve` is computed with balances and only excess over the target reserve is shifted out.
hypotheses.impact: Positive rebase / accidental transfers accrued to the Well (which the docs claim are skim/sync-able) are directly extractable by a third party via `shift`, and worse — `shift` uses `_calcReserve` parametrised by `totalSupply()`, so any drift between reserves and balances lets the caller drain the invariant contribution from LPs.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require that shift's caller supplies the shifting input, or restrict shift to amounts equal to the difference between stored reserves and balances (i.e. only "excess" tokens) so a caller cannot shift LP-owned value.

hypotheses.title: Aquifer.boreWell init call can be front-run to initialize Well with attacker-controlled name/symbol
hypotheses.description: `boreWell` deploys a Well clone and then calls `initFunctionCall` on it. If `initFunctionCall` is empty, the Well is deployed uninitialized. An attacker can front-run the legitimate `init` call (or call `init` themselves if the Well is deployed without init data) to set a malicious name/symbol or, in the case of `WellUpgradeable`, call `initNoWellToken` to lock the Well. Since `boreWell` checks `isInitialized()` after the init call, an attacker who front-runs with their own init will cause the legitimate `boreWell` to revert (WellNotInitialized or already initialized), or worse, the attacker's init succeeds and the Well is permanently misconfigured.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1. Legitimate user calls `boreWell` with `initFunctionCall` empty (or with a salt that allows prediction). 2. Attacker front-runs by calling `init` on the predicted Well address with malicious parameters. 3. The legitimate `boreWell` call then fails because the Well is already initialized, or the Well is initialized with attacker-controlled data.
hypotheses.impact: Well deployed with attacker-controlled name/symbol; legitimate deployment blocked; potential phishing via misleading token names.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `initFunctionCall` to be non-empty in `boreWell`, or use `create2` with a salt that includes `msg.sender` (already done) and ensure init is atomic.

hypotheses.title: MultiFlowPump.update can be called by anyone for any well
hypotheses.description: `update` is permissionless and reads `IWell(well).getReserves()` only in the read paths, but during `update` the caller supplies the `reserves` array directly and it is stored as the pump's last reserves for the caller's `msg.sender`. Any external caller can call `update` with arbitrary reserve values for `msg.sender` (which normally would be the Well during a swap). Because `_getSlotForAddress(msg.sender)` stores per-caller, calling `update` from an arbitrary address just creates a dormant record for that address; it does not corrupt the well's record. However, `_init` is executed with `lastTimestamp == 0` on first update and can write arbitrary reserves for `msg.sender`. An untrusted actor calling `update` on the pump for an address they control cannot affect other wells.
hypotheses.attackPath: No cross-well impact; storage is per-caller.
hypotheses.impact: None on other wells.
hypotheses.recommendation: Optionally restrict `update` to the Well via a caller check.

hypotheses.title: MultiFlowPump `_getDeltaTimestamp` wraps uint40 in 2106
hypotheses.description: `_getDeltaTimestamp` casts `block.timestamp` to `uint40` and subtracts `lastTimestamp` (also uint40). This is fine until block.timestamp exceeds 2^40 (~year 36,000), but more importantly the cast is done before subtraction so any `lastTimestamp` stored as uint40 read from storage also fits. The real off-by-one/edge concern is that if `block.timestamp == lastTimestamp`, `deltaTimestamp == 0` and callers correctly skip. No bug today, but the design assumes `block.timestamp` never wraps.
hypotheses.attackPath: No current attack; exploited only after timestamp wrap (~1e12), far beyond practical horizon.
hypotheses.impact: None currently; theoretical miscomputation of cumulative/EMA values after year ~36,000.
hypotheses.recommendation: Document the assumption or widen the stored timestamp type.

hypotheses.title: Sigma/helper—Aquifer salt replay across deployments with same salt
hypotheses.description: `salt = keccak256(abi.encode(msg.sender, salt))` mixes caller, but does not include the implementation or immutable data. Reusing the same salt with the same implementation and same immutable data will collide and revert. This is a determinism property, not a vulnerability: an attacker cannot cause harm because they can only affect their own deployments.
hypotheses.attackPath: Not exploitable to harm others.
hypotheses.impact: Self-inflicted DoS only.
hypotheses.recommendation: Consider including the implementation address in the salt for clarity.

hypotheses.title: Missing nonce and chainId in ERC20Permit signed data
hypotheses.description: `Well` inherits `ERC20PermitUpgradeable` and exposes `permit` via `__ERC20Permit_init` without sealing a domain separator keyed to the contract address and chain at initialization. `ERC20PermitUpgradeable` uses the EIP-712 domain derived at call-time, so signing data is bound to the current chainid and verifying contract; however the Well itself is deployed via clone with `ClonePlus` and `init` is callable only once, so a clone reused across chains is not directly at issue. The primary concern is that `init` on the implementation is disabled (`_disableInitializers`) but on clones the `__ERC20Permit_init(_name)` sets a name but the standard permit nonce is per-account and stored, which is fine. No exploit under external adversary assumptions.
hypotheses.attackPath: An attacker cannot replay a permit because the domain separator includes the contract address and chain id; nonces are tracked by `ERC20PermitUpgradeable`.
hypotheses.impact: None reproducible.
hypotheses.recommendation: Confirm domain separator uses EIP-712 with name, version, chainId, verifying contract; add explicit chainId if upgrading.

hypotheses.title: WellUpgradeable init does not bind domain separator to upgraded implementation
hypotheses.description: `init` is `reinitializer(2)`, and `initNoWellToken` sets `initializer` to version 1. Since these are used by `LibWellUpgradeableConstructor` and externally via Aquifer, the ERC20Permit domain separator is derived at signature verification time using the current `address(this)` and chainId, so replays across clones are not possible. The concern is a stale permit signed against a pre-upgrade domain only if `name`/version changes, which would invalidate prior signatures rather than enable a replay.
hypotheses.attackPath: No external attack path identified within the rules.
hypotheses.impact: None concrete.
hypotheses.recommendation: Explicitly document that name changes invalidate outstanding permits.
